slides.title: CB1 activation rapidly changes a neuronal growth cone
body: A **growth cone** is the moving structure at the tip of a growing axon. Its internal actin network helps the tip extend, change shape, and respond to local signals. Roland and colleagues followed growth cones in cultured hippocampal neurons while applying **WIN 55,212-2**, a synthetic agonist that activates cannabinoid receptors.

After WIN exposure, the growth cones retracted toward the cell body instead of continuing their earlier advance. Retraction began within a few minutes and typically approached a plateau over the following minutes. The fluorescent labels allowed movement of the actin-rich tip to be followed in the same neuron before and after the chemical was added.

A CB1-blocking drug prevented the retraction, while removing WIN allowed growth-cone movement to recover in the tested condition. The change depended on continuing receptor-sensitive signaling and could be reversible. CB1 activation was therefore altering the forces that controlled the growing tip, producing a physical movement of neuronal structure rather than only changing transmitter release at a synapse.

slides.title: Myosin contributes to cannabinoid-induced retraction
body: Actin filaments help form the growth cone's internal framework, while **non-muscle myosin II** generates force against those filaments. The motor uses energy from ATP to pull within the actin network. When this contraction becomes strong enough, the growing tip can retract toward the axon instead of continuing to extend away from the cell body.

In the cannabinoid study, CB1 activation increased phosphorylation of a protein that regulates myosin activity. **ROCK**, an enzyme that promotes actin–myosin contraction, was part of the signaling pathway required for retraction. The receptor's chemical response was therefore converted into greater activity of machinery that could generate physical force inside the neuronal process.

The researchers applied **blebbistatin**, which inhibits myosin II, before activating CB1 receptors. Growth-cone retraction was strongly reduced. The agonist was still available, but the motor could no longer produce its usual response. Blocking ROCK also reduced retraction, interrupting an earlier signaling step that would normally promote the contraction of the actin–myosin network.

slides.title: Cannabinoid activation also changes growth cones in slices
body: An **organotypic slice** is a tissue preparation kept alive outside the animal while preserving part of its original cellular arrangement. The cannabinoid researchers examined axons growing from cortical tissue in these slices. This allowed growth-cone movement to be followed while the axons remained among neighboring cells and tissue structures rather than growing as isolated neurons on a dish.

Applying WIN also caused actin-rich growth cones in the slices to retract. The response was observed in a preparation containing more of the developing brain's local structure. Fluorescent labeling distinguished the growing processes, allowing their positions to be followed through time as the receptor agonist reached the tissue and the tips changed their direction of movement.

Growth cones with additional CB1 expression showed a stronger response, while axons relying on their naturally expressed receptors also responded. Retraction developed more slowly in slices than in isolated cultures. The authors attributed part of that delay to the time required for the highly lipid-soluble compound to diffuse through tissue before reaching its receptor targets.

slides.title: Cytoskeletal inhibitors separate contraction from transport
body: Actin and microtubules contribute differently to a growing axon's shape and movement. Actin forms a flexible network near the growth cone, while microtubules provide internal support and transport tracks. During cannabinoid-induced retraction, actin became organized into straighter bundles and nearby microtubules bent. These changes were consistent with force acting on the internal framework rather than simple withdrawal of the membrane alone.

The researchers disrupted microtubules with **nocodazole**. This stopped normal growth-cone advance, but WIN could still cause the tip to retract. Microtubules were therefore needed for normal forward growth without being essential for the drug-induced pullback. The same structure can contribute to extension while a different part of the cytoskeleton supplies the force for contraction.

Disrupting actin with **cytochalasin D** reduced both forward growth and cannabinoid-induced retraction. Inhibiting myosin also reduced retraction. Together, these interventions identified an actin–myosin force-generating process: the receptor activated intracellular signaling, the motor pulled against actin, and the neuronal process shortened. Removing the actin network or disabling the motor interrupted that physical response.

slides.title: Lipid messengers can signal back toward a nerve terminal
body: At some synapses, the receiving neuron can send a chemical signal back to the releasing terminal. Activity in the postsynaptic cell stimulates endocannabinoid production, and the lipid messenger reaches presynaptic CB1 receptors. This is called **retrograde signaling** because the chemical influence travels in the opposite direction from the usual transmitter message across that synapse.

Activating presynaptic CB1 receptors can reduce calcium entry and weaken the processes that release transmitter. The next action potential then produces less chemical output from the affected terminal. The receiving neuron can consequently reduce some of the input reaching it by making a messenger that acts back on the axon supplying that input.

The effect on the wider circuit depends on the terminal being suppressed. Reducing glutamate release can decrease excitatory input, while reducing GABA release can remove inhibition and make a receiving neuron more responsive. In both cases, the direct action is reduced transmitter release. The different circuit effects arise because the suppressed terminals normally perform different functions.

slides.title: Chloride gradients determine an anion channel's effect
body: Opening a chloride channel does not produce the same electrical effect in every neuron. The response depends on the **chloride gradient**, the difference in concentration across the membrane. Transport proteins establish that gradient by moving ions into or out of the cell. Opening the channel then allows current that moves voltage toward the level favored by this distribution.

When chloride-channel opening makes the inside more negative, the response is called **hyperpolarization**. This often reduces firing during the immediate input. The same voltage change can also affect other channels. Some sodium channels become unavailable during sustained depolarization and recover from that state when the membrane becomes more negative, increasing the number available for a later response.

A neuron can therefore become more negative at rest while responding more strongly to a subsequent stimulus. The immediate voltage shift and later action-potential output are different measurements. In retinal ganglion cells, cannabinoid-sensitive changes in chloride handling produced this combination, making the effect of the channel depend on both the ion gradient and the neuron's recent membrane voltage.

slides.title: A cannabinoid study measures visual behavior in tadpoles
body: **Retinal ganglion cells** carry the retina's output toward the brain. Miraucourt and colleagues examined how cannabinoid signaling changed these neurons and visual behavior in **Xenopus** tadpoles. The animals swam freely above a screen displaying moving dark dots. Researchers tracked their movements to measure whether they avoided a dot as it approached them.

Under brighter **photopic** conditions, control tadpoles responded to visible dark dots with rapid avoidance movements. The recording follows the animal and the moving target in the same view. Measuring the encounter and the change in swimming made it possible to distinguish an avoidance response from movement that occurred while no target was approaching.

The researchers varied dot visibility by changing illumination and contrast, the difference in brightness between target and background. They also measured responses to a uniform background before presenting visible targets. These conditions established how often a rapid movement occurred without a detectable dot, providing a comparison for the later avoidance behavior under different visual conditions.

slides.title: CB1 activation improves vision under dim illumination
body: Under **mesopic** conditions, an intermediate range of dim illumination, untreated tadpoles often failed to avoid the moving dots reliably. Tadpoles treated with WIN responded more successfully under the same low-light conditions. The drug therefore changed performance when the visual target was difficult to detect, rather than requiring a different kind of stimulus or movement response.

The researchers also recorded stronger light-evoked firing in retinal ganglion cells after cannabinoid receptor activation. These neurons supply visual information to the brain, so changing their response can alter the sensory signal available before an avoidance movement is selected. The behavioral improvement occurred alongside a measured change in the output neurons of the visual system.

Ordinary swimming speed between dot encounters was similar in control and treated animals. Treated tadpoles, however, produced faster movements during successful escapes. Increasing endogenous cannabinoid availability also improved dim-light avoidance, and blocking CB1 prevented that benefit. Both receptor activation and preservation of the body's own cannabinoid messenger could therefore change performance in this particular visual task.

slides.title: Cannabinoids change chloride-dependent excitability
body: The retinal study identified a change in chloride handling inside ganglion cells. CB1 activation reduced intracellular chloride through a pathway involving **NKCC1**, a transporter that normally brings chloride into the cell. Less chloride accumulated inside, changing the electrical effect of chloride-permeable channels. Fluorescent chloride measurements allowed this internal ion change to be followed during drug exposure.

The shift made the resting membrane potential more negative through chloride currents controlled by **glycine**, another neurotransmitter. This hyperpolarization increased the availability of sodium channels for later activation. When the cell subsequently received a depolarizing stimulus, it could produce more action potentials. A more negative resting voltage therefore occurred together with a stronger response to a later input in these retinal neurons.

The researchers observed hyperpolarization in isolated ganglion cells as well as altered responses in the retina. Blocking CB1 prevented the voltage change, and blocking glycine receptors prevented the usual increase in visual responsiveness. The chemical effect involved the receiving cell's ion transport and channels, which changed how visual input was converted into firing before the signal traveled onward to the brain.

slides.title: Receptor activation changes the mechanical state of a cell
body: Cannabinoid signaling can also change the shape of the cell body. Roland and colleagues examined **Neuro2A cells**, a cultured neural cell line that grows identifiable processes. After CB1 activation, these processes retracted and the cell body became rounder. Actin accumulated beneath the membrane and near the ends of the retracting processes as the cell changed shape.

The researchers measured **stiffness**, the cell's resistance to being deformed. A small probe pressed against the cell surface, allowing that resistance to be compared before and after treatment. CB1 activation produced a temporary increase in stiffness alongside the structural changes. The response therefore included a measurable change in the cell's physical properties, not only a change in its outline.

Inhibiting myosin with blebbistatin prevented the usual cell-rounding response. Myosin normally generates force against the actin network beneath the membrane, so reducing its activity weakens the contraction. The agonist could still reach the receptor, but the physical response was interrupted downstream. Receptor signaling had changed cell shape by engaging an internal network capable of producing mechanical force.

slides.title: Agonists differ in receptor uptake and cellular tolerance
body: Agonists that activate the same opioid receptor can differ in how strongly they promote its removal from the surface. DAMGO produced substantial mu-receptor uptake in cultured axons. Morphine produced little detectable rapid uptake, yet prolonged morphine exposure still reduced receptor availability and weakened presynaptic inhibition. Its slower effects differed from those measured immediately after the drug was applied.

Two other agonists, **PZM21** and **TRV130**, produced little detectable receptor uptake and did not produce the same tolerance after the tested prolonged treatment. These compounds favored some receptor-signaling responses more than others. An agonist's ability to activate a receptor initially therefore need not match its ability to promote the cellular processes that later reduce responsiveness.

Blocking GRK2 and GRK3 also prevented the tolerance produced by prolonged morphine treatment in this preparation. These enzymes add phosphate groups that regulate the receptor's movement and availability. The later loss of opioid responsiveness depended partly on that regulatory process, even though morphine had produced little measurable rapid uptake during the shorter initial observation period.

slides.title: Cannabinoids reshape several neuronal compartments
body: Cannabinoids can change neuronal shape by activating **CB1 receptors**. Researchers examined cultured hippocampal neurons and followed changes in the cell body and **dendrites**, the branches that receive signals from other neurons. These structures form the **somatodendritic region**. After receptor activation, outer dendritic branches retracted while portions nearer the cell body broadened, changing the shape of this region within minutes.

These changes involve **actin**, a protein that forms part of the **cytoskeleton**, the internal framework that supports the cell and helps it change shape. CB1 activation reorganized actin into straighter bundles as nearby microtubules bent. Following the same neuron over several minutes revealed how this internal reorganization accompanied physical changes in its dendrites and the region around its cell body.

Brief activation changed shape within minutes, while overnight treatment reduced the number of developing dendrites. Researchers examined these outcomes separately because immediate contraction and longer-term growth are different processes. Blocking ROCK or myosin prevented the overnight reduction. The chemical changed neuronal structure through a pathway that regulated the cell's internal framework and the development of its branches over different timescales.

items.text: Absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion govern the amount of drug reaching a target. Membrane permeability and transporters also determine access to receptors inside cells.

items.lead: Binding and response are separate properties.
items.text: Affinity describes binding, potency describes the amount needed for an effect, and efficacy describes the response a drug can produce. Agonists activate receptors; antagonists prevent activation.

items.lead: Synaptic drugs act at several steps.
items.text: Synthesis, vesicle storage, release, receptor activation, reuptake, and enzymatic breakdown each provide targets for changing neurotransmission.
Tolerance reduces a response to the same exposure, whereas sensitization increases it. Receptor trafficking and cellular adaptations can change signaling during repeated treatment.

items.lead: Transmitter identity does not specify one behavior.
items.text: Glutamate, GABA, acetylcholine, monoamines, peptides, and lipid messengers act through distinct receptors and pathways. Receptor location and circuit target determine the resulting cellular and behavioral effects.

Identify the manipulated molecule, the affected cell, and the measured response. Receptor imaging, transmitter sensors, pathway targeting, and behavioral recordings reveal different steps in a drug’s action.
